claims.text: At high temperatures, overall wear resistance of a FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating is governed by formation of a continuous, adherent protective oxide scale.
Copper segregation at grain boundaries promotes rapid formation of the protective oxide scale.
The protective oxide scale reduces mechanical wear by suppressing microcracking and spallation.
A controlled heat treatment can promote copper segregation at grain boundaries.
Deposition-induced grain refinement can promote copper segregation at grain boundaries.
Enhanced copper segregation leads to formation of a continuous and adherent oxide layer.
Chromium oxidation contributes to formation of the protective oxide layer.
Copper and chromium preferentially oxidize at grain boundaries.
An adherent oxide scale acts as a mechanical barrier against friction-induced crack initiation and propagation.
An adherent oxide scale reduces material spallation during high-temperature wear.
The treated coating will have a lower wear rate than the as-deposited baseline under identical high-temperature wear conditions.
The treated coating will exhibit smoother wear tracks than the baseline.
A coherent protective oxide scale will form earlier in the treated coating than in the baseline.
The as-deposited baseline is expected to form a less uniform or slower-forming oxide scale.
The proposed mechanism is applicable at approximately 500°C to 700°C when oxidation is active and loading does not destabilize the coating.
At substantially lower temperatures, protective oxide formation may be too slow.
At substantially higher temperatures, the coating may degrade irrespective of oxide protection.
